source_text: A jury in Wisconsin has found a man guilty of election fraud and identity theft for requesting the ballots of Republican state Assembly Speaker Robin Vos and Democratic Racine Mayor Cory Mason without their consent. A Racine County jury on Tuesday found Harry Wait guilty of two misdemeanor election fraud charges and one felony identity theft charge following a two-day trial. He was acquitted of a second count of identity theft. Wait leads a group that makes false election claims. He admitted in 2022 that he requested the ballots to try to prove that the state’s voter registration system is vulnerable to fraud.
rewritten_text:
A Wisconsin jury found Harry Wait guilty of requesting the ballots of Robin Vos and Cory Mason without their consent—two misdemeanor election-fraud counts and one felony identity-theft count, though he was acquitted of another identity-theft charge. His conduct was wrong: election rules must be respected, and nobody should take it upon himself to obtain someone else’s ballot.

But Wait said he was trying to test whether the voter-registration system was vulnerable. That claim doesn’t prove there was a vulnerability, and his group has made false election claims. Still, protecting public confidence means taking security concerns seriously, not treating every challenge to the system as beyond discussion. The law has delivered its verdict; officials should also make clear that the rules are secure and fairly enforced.

source_text: Organizers are claiming 8 million people attended “No Kings” protests at more than 3,300 events, but there’s no official count from US authorities. That makes the headline number a political estimate, not a verified tally. The protests show a determined opposition to President Trump, but turning dissent into a spectacle against an elected leader doesn’t make it a mandate to override the voters or weaken the country’s institutions.
rewritten_text: Organizers say 8 million people joined “No Kings” protests at more than 3,300 events. There’s no official count, so the figure is an estimate—not a verified tally—but that uncertainty shouldn’t be used to dismiss the scale of the dissent. Protesting an elected leader isn’t overriding voters; it’s a basic part of democracy, especially when people fear their rights and institutions are at risk. The real question is whether those institutions protect everyone, not whether people are allowed to challenge those in power.
